records.rawDisplayText:
Here is the complete, detailed breakdown of how /proc works, combining the core technical mechanisms that made the concept click.1. What /proc Actually Is/proc (the Proc filesystem or procfs) is a pseudo-filesystem managed directly by the Linux kernel.Storage: It uses 0 bytes of disk space. It exists entirely within system RAM.Interface: Instead of inventing custom system calls or complex administrative software to show system metrics, Linux presents kernel data using standard file operations (open(), read(), close()).Design Philosophy: It implements the core Linux principle: "Everything is a file."2. The On-Demand Generation Mechanism (On the Fly)The text inside a /proc file does not exist in memory until a program or user explicitly asks for it.How the kernel keeps track of data continuously:The kernel constantly updates raw binary state variables in RAM (e.g., tracking total RAM, CPU cycles, or active network connections inside C structures). It does not spend CPU cycles continuously updating text strings like "MemTotal: 16384000 kB" in the background.What happens step-by-step when you access a file:System Call: You run a command (like cat /proc/meminfo) or a program issues an open() followed by a read() system call on a /proc path.Kernel Interception: The storage drive (SSD/HDD) is completely bypassed. The Linux VFS (Virtual Filesystem) intercepts the call and routes it to the procfs driver.Execution: The kernel executes a specific internal function attached to that file path.Formatting: That function reads the current binary variables directly out of kernel RAM, translates them into plain ASCII text, and dumps that text into a temporary memory buffer.Delivery & Cleanup: The text buffer is sent to your program output. As soon as the file descriptor is closed, that generated text buffer is discarded.If a file in /proc is never read, that formatted text is never created.3. PIDs and Process Life Cycles (/proc/[PID])Every running process on the system is represented in kernel memory by a structure called task_struct.When a process with PID 23 is running:The raw data: The process state, memory addresses, environment variables, and open file descriptors exist continuously in kernel RAM inside PID 23's task_struct.The path: /proc/23/ exists as a valid access route.Reading process files: When you read a file like /proc/23/status or /proc/23/cmdline, the kernel looks up PID 23's task_struct, converts its binary values into ASCII text on the spot, and returns it.Termination: The exact millisecond PID 23 finishes executing, the kernel frees its task_struct. The path /proc/23/ immediately stops responding and vanishes from directory listings.4. How System Utilities Depend on /procStandard Linux monitoring and diagnostic tools do not have direct access to internal kernel memory. Instead, they act as text parsers for /proc.When you run these tools, they execute a simple workflow: open the corresponding /proc file, read the generated ASCII text, parse the numbers, and format them nicely on your terminal.+----------------+      System Call       +------------------------+
| Linux Utility  | ---------------------> |      Linux Kernel      |
|  (e.g., free)  |                        |  (Reads C Structures)  |
+----------------+                        +------------------------+
        ^                                             |
        |                                             |
        |          Formats into ASCII Text            |
        +---------------------------------------------+
CommandWhat it actually reads behind the scenesps / topScans /proc/ for numerical folders, then reads /proc/[PID]/stat, /proc/[PID]/status, and /proc/[PID]/cmdline.freeOpens /proc/meminfo, parses lines like MemTotal and MemAvailable, and calculates usable RAM.uptimeReads /proc/uptime to get raw seconds since system boot and idle time.lscpuReads /proc/cpuinfo to display CPU model, core count, and cache sizes.
